saturated_angles: Generic 'teal and orange' grade with no rationale
Cutting on every single beat of the music (mechanical, not felt)
"Cinematic" used as a synonym for black bars alone with no shot-language change
underserved_gaps: How to build a cinematic edit from a large, chronologically messy personal archive (282 clips, no shot list) rather than a planned single-location shoot
How to structure a multi-week road trip (not a single destination) into one coherent emotional arc

data_points.claim: Viewer retention on YouTube is roughly 70% for videos under 2 minutes and drops below 50% past the 2-minute mark; 2–3 minutes is widely described as an awkward retention middle ground — creators are advised to either stay under ~2 minutes or commit to a longer 6–12+ minute format.
data_points.usable_as: flag_for_proposal_stage — worth surfacing to the user before locking final runtime, even though 2-3min was the initial preference

data_points.claim: Editors recommend using a driving music beat as the pacing base layer, then deliberately breaking from the beat-cut grid for emotional or scenic moments — cutting on literally every beat reads as mechanical rather than felt.
data_points.source_name: Filmmaking for Journalists — pacing & rhythm notes
data_points.usable_as: edit_decisions guidance — vary cut rhythm around the beat grid

data_points.claim: A cinematic color base is typically built from correction first (accurate exposure/white balance), then creative grading (e.g. lifted shadows, tamed highlights, added midtone contrast, teal-orange or soft split-toning) rather than a single LUT alone.
data_points.source_name: Surfaced Studio — cinematic color correction tutorial

data_points.claim: Travel edits commonly vary pace deliberately: fast cuts through transit/landscape coverage, then a deliberate slow-down (longer hold, sometimes slow motion) at the actual landmark or payoff moment.

common_questions: How do I turn hundreds of random phone clips into one coherent story instead of a random slideshow?
What music actually fits an 'epic' travel mood without sounding like a generic stock trailer?
How long should a personal trip recap actually be so people watch the whole thing?

misconceptions.myth: Adding black bars and a LUT is what makes footage 'cinematic.'
misconceptions.reality: Cinematic quality comes from shot selection, pacing, and an emotional arc — letterboxing and a LUT are surface dressing on top of that.

misconceptions.myth: Cutting exactly on every beat of the music produces the most 'epic' feeling edit.
misconceptions.reality: Constant beat-locked cutting reads as mechanical; the strongest edits break from the grid at meaningful moments.

audience_insights.knowledge_level: User is a first-time cinematic editor of their own footage — comfortable directing high-level creative choices (mood, platform, length) but relying on the agent for genre conventions (grading, pacing, structure).
pain_points: 282 raw clips (13GB) with no existing shot list or grouping — the raw-footage-to-story gap is the main obstacle

research_brief.research_summary: The strongest available direction is a hybrid: adopt the genre-standard 'epic cinematic travel' grammar (correction-then-grade color, driving music as the pacing spine, letterboxing reserved for key reveals) but structure it around the trip's actual chaptered, multi-week, multi-location reality rather than a single continuous mood — and deliberately break from beat-locked cutting at landmark payoffs so it feels felt, not mechanical. One data point worth flagging before locking length: 2–3 minutes is a documented retention danger zone on YouTube (steep drop-off vs. sub-2-minute or 6–12-minute formats) — worth a quick gut-check with the user before compose, not a reason to override their stated preference.
